# Thesis: hyperscaler (hyperscaler@v4)

## Thesis

The hyperscalers are the buyers. Their capex is the AI buildout, and the server and network category of PP&E is where the GPUs land. Capex allocation is the measure that matters most here; project-level investment (named campuses, power deals, cloud commitments to neoclouds, third-party-financed ventures) and plans versus reality (capex guidance against the actual) matter next. Revenue exposure matters least: these companies sell ads, software and cloud, and no reported segment is the AI one. The signal to watch is the year-on-year growth in the gross value of the server and network category, read against the company's own capex guidance and against purchase commitments and leases not yet commenced, which run a year or more ahead.

The scale, from the filings read for this version: the four largest spent $360 billion of cash capex in their 2025 fiscal years (Amazon $131.8 billion, Alphabet $91.4 billion, Meta $69.7 billion, Microsoft $64.6 billion for the year to June 2025), and Microsoft's year to June 2026 was $115.9 billion. Dell'Oro puts the top four US cloud providers at over $340 billion of data-center capex in 2025, up 76 percent, and forecasts worldwide data-center capex above $1 trillion in 2026. Guidance for 2026 is Amazon about $200 billion, Alphabet $175 to $185 billion, Meta $115 to $135 billion.

## Companies

Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META) and Oracle (ORCL). The first four are the model: huge capex, a server category in the PP&E note, guidance "to support AI". Oracle sits at the edge: it is a hyperscaler by spend but its buildout is contracted to one customer class, its remaining performance obligations are the forward number, and customers now prepay or supply the GPUs; a reader should treat it as a buyer with a seller's backlog. Apple and Tesla also buy compute but do not report like this; they sit in `other`.

Microsoft. No AI segment. Reported segments are Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing; the PP&E category is "Servers, network equipment, and software", $215,874 million gross at June 30 2026 against $132,836 million at June 30 2025 (FY2026 10-K, Note on property and equipment). Cash additions to property and equipment were $115,948 million in FY2026 and $64,551 million in FY2025 (FY2026 10-K cash flow statement). Stated AI revenue: "Our AI business surpassed an annual revenue run rate of $37 billion, up 123% year-over-year" (Q3 FY2026 release, April 29 2026); the Q4 FY2026 release of July 29 2026 gave no AI run rate. No stated AI share of capex as of 2026-10-29 (FY2026 10-K and the July 29 2026 release checked). Finance lease liabilities $66,594 million at June 30 2026 ($4,290 current, $62,304 non-current) against $46,172 million a year earlier; leases not yet commenced $329.1 billion "primarily for datacenters" (FY2026 10-K, leases note). Commercial remaining performance obligation $678 billion, up 84 percent (FY2026 10-K MD&A). In the layer because it buys the compute and reports it in a server category.

Alphabet. No AI segment. Segments are Google Services, Google Cloud, Other Bets. The PP&E category is "Technical infrastructure", $203,679 million gross at December 31 2025 against $141,852 million at December 31 2024, with "Assets not yet in service" $78,592 million against $50,597 million (FY2025 10-K, supplemental financial information note). Purchases of property and equipment $91,447 million in 2025 and $52,535 million in 2024 (FY2025 10-K cash flow statement). Stated split on the Q4 2025 call: "approximately 60% of that investment in servers, and 40% in data centers and networking equipment" (Ashkenazi, February 4 2026). 2026 guidance $175 to $185 billion (same call) and the 10-K says "In 2026, we expect to significantly increase, relative to 2025, our investment in our technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers." Remaining performance obligations $242.8 billion at December 31 2025, half expected within 24 months (FY2025 10-K revenue note); Pichai gave Cloud backlog as $240 billion on the call. Purchase commitments and other contractual obligations $149.1 billion at December 31 2025, $113.0 billion short term (FY2025 10-K MD&A). No stated AI dollar amount or share of capex or revenue as of 2026-10-29 (FY2025 10-K and Q4 2025 call checked). In the layer because technical infrastructure is 60 percent of gross PP&E and the servers are the AI fleet.

Amazon. No AI segment. Segments are North America, International, AWS; AWS net sales $128,725 million in 2025, up 20 percent (FY2025 10-K). The PP&E category is "Servers and networking equipment", $172,492 million gross at December 31 2025 against $113,156 million at December 31 2024; "Construction in progress" $71,745 million against $46,636 million (FY2025 10-K, property and equipment note). Purchases of property and equipment $131,819 million in 2025 and $82,999 million in 2024; net of proceeds and incentives $128,320 million and $77,658 million (FY2025 10-K cash flow and the February 5 2026 release). The release says the $50.7 billion increase in net purchases "primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence"; the 10-K MD&A says cash capex "primarily reflect investments in technology infrastructure" with the majority supporting AWS. Jassy, February 5 2026: "we expect to invest about $200 billion in capital expenditures across Amazon in 2026". Remaining performance obligations for contracts over one year $244.0 billion at December 31 2025, weighted average life about four years (FY2025 10-K). Finance lease liabilities $12,286 million at December 31 2025 (FY2025 10-K leases note). No stated AI share or amount of capex as of 2026-10-29 (FY2025 10-K and the February 5 2026 release checked); "primarily reflects investments in AI" is qualitative. In the layer because its server category and AWS carry the largest capex of the five.

Meta. No AI segment. Segments are Family of Apps and Reality Labs. The PP&E category is "Servers and network assets", $98,040 million gross at December 31 2025 against $68,397 million at December 31 2024; "Construction in progress" $50,521 million against $26,802 million (FY2025 10-K, Note 6). Purchases of property and equipment $69,691 million in 2025 and $37,256 million in 2024; principal payments on finance leases $2,524 million and $1,969 million; the company's own capex line, which includes those principal payments, was $72.22 billion for 2025 (FY2025 10-K cash flow; January 28 2026 release). Guidance: "We anticipate making capital expenditures of approximately $115 billion to $135 billion in 2026 to support our AI efforts and core business" (FY2025 10-K MD&A; the release ties it to Meta Superintelligence Labs). Contractual commitments $131.05 billion at December 31 2025, "mostly related to third-party cloud capacity arrangements", $30.63 billion due in 2026; leases not yet commenced about $103.77 billion, mostly data centers, commencing 2026 to 2030 (FY2025 10-K). The Louisiana data center campus venture: Meta holds 20 percent, equity method, estimated development costs $27,000 million, maximum exposure to loss $45,950 million, assets of $4,300 million contributed and a $2,554 million distribution received (FY2025 10-K, non-marketable equity investments note). No stated AI share or amount of capex or revenue as of 2026-10-29 (FY2025 10-K and the January 28 2026 release checked). In the layer because it buys the compute at hyperscaler scale with no cloud to sell it through.

Oracle. No AI segment; the cloud line is "cloud infrastructure" (IaaS) inside Cloud and license. Cloud infrastructure was 53 percent of total cloud revenue in fiscal 2026, 42 percent in fiscal 2025 (FY2026 10-K); Q4 FY2026 cloud infrastructure revenue $5.8 billion, up 93 percent (June 10 2026 release). The PP&E category is "Computer, network, machinery and equipment", $59,634 million gross at May 31 2026 against $30,345 million at May 31 2025; "Construction in progress" $39,973 million against $16,510 million (FY2026 10-K PP&E note). Capital expenditures $55,663 million in fiscal 2026 and $21,215 million in fiscal 2025 (FY2026 10-K cash flow statement). Remaining performance obligations $638 billion at May 31 2026, up 363 percent; "prepaid and customer-supplied hardware portions of large AI contracts" total $75 billion, which the company says "substantially reduces the amount of capital Oracle must raise" (June 10 2026 release). Finance lease liabilities $7,701 million at May 31 2026; additional operating lease commitments not yet commenced $260 billion with 15 to 19 year terms; unconditional purchase obligations $13,309 million plus $19,000 million signed June 22 2026 (FY2026 10-K leases and commitments note). No stated AI share or amount of capex as of 2026-10-29 (FY2026 10-K and the June 10 2026 release checked); the release gives no capex guidance. In the layer because its capex, leases and RPO are the AI data-center buildout, contracted ahead.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Capex** (`values.capex`, cash paid for property and equipment) is the main line, but it understates the buildout: finance leases (`facts.finance_lease_liability`: Microsoft $66.6 billion, Amazon $12.3 billion, Oracle $7.7 billion at the latest year-end), leases not yet commenced (Microsoft $329.1 billion, Oracle $260 billion, Meta $103.8 billion) and third-party-funded datacenters (Meta's Louisiana venture, 20 percent owned, $27 billion to build) sit outside it. Meta's own capex figure includes finance lease principal; the ledger's `values.capex` does not.
2. **PP&E by category** (`facts.ppe_category`): the server category (Microsoft "Servers, network equipment, and software"; Meta "Servers and network assets"; Alphabet "Technical infrastructure", called "Information technology assets" before the FY2024 10-K, the same category renamed; Amazon "Servers and networking equipment"; Oracle "Computer, network, machinery and equipment") is where GPUs land. Its year-on-year growth in gross value is the hard number closest to compute capex: Microsoft +$83.0 billion in FY2026, Alphabet +$61.8 billion, Amazon +$59.3 billion, Meta +$29.6 billion in 2025, Oracle +$29.3 billion in FY2026. Buildings, land and construction in progress are the shell, not AI as such; construction in progress is large (Amazon $71.7 billion, Meta $50.5 billion, Oracle $40.0 billion) and mixed.
3. **What the company says** (`ai_spend`): these companies give total-capex guidance "to support AI" (`scope: total`: Meta $115 to $135 billion for 2026, Alphabet $175 to $185 billion, Amazon about $200 billion) and, on calls, sometimes a split (Alphabet: about 60 percent servers, 40 percent data centers and networking, Q4 2025 call). An explicit AI share from the company (`scope: ai`, `explicit_share`) beats any estimate; none of the five gave one in the filings read.
4. **Purchase commitments** (`facts.purchase_commitments`) are forward: contracted GPUs and cloud capacity (Meta $131.0 billion, mostly third-party cloud capacity; Alphabet $149.1 billion). A jump in commitments precedes capex by a year. Remaining performance obligations (Microsoft $678 billion, Oracle $638 billion, Amazon $244 billion, Alphabet $243 billion) are demand, not spend; they belong in `basis`.

## How to attribute

Capex, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share`: the company states the AI (or GPU/server) share of capex → `ai_amount = share × capex`. Alphabet's "approximately 60% ... in servers" is a server share, not an AI share; use it only as `ppe_category` support, confidence ≤ 0.6, and name the call.
- `stated_amount`: the company states an AI dollar amount for the year (`scope: ai`, `explicit_amount`). None of the five did in the filings read for this version.
- `ppe_category`: growth in the server/network category: `ai_amount = category gross(t) − category gross(t−1)`, when both years are in `facts`. Name the category. This counts all server growth, not only AI; say so in `basis` and set confidence ≤ 0.6.
- `qualitative`: the company says "primarily AI" (Amazon's "primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence", Meta's "to support our AI efforts and core business") but gives nothing to compute from: no amount, confidence ≤ 0.3.
- `none`: nothing links spend to AI.

Opex: AI shows up as depreciation of the fleet (Alphabet $21.1 billion in 2025, up 38 percent) and as R&D headcount; no hyperscaler quantifies the AI part. Expect `qualitative` or `none` for opex.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_amount`: the company states an AI revenue figure for the year. Microsoft's $37 billion AI run rate (April 29 2026) is a run-rate, not a fiscal-year figure; confidence ≤ 0.5 and say so in `basis`.
- `stated_share`: the company states AI's share of revenue, or of a segment's growth. A growth contribution ("AI contributed N points to Azure growth") is not a share of revenue; record it in `basis`, not as a share. Confidence ≤ 0.8 for a true share.
- `segment`: not available. Microsoft Intelligent Cloud is not AI; Google Cloud ($58.7 billion in 2025) is not AI; AWS ($128.7 billion) is not AI; Oracle's cloud infrastructure line is not AI. Never sum a cloud segment as the AI line.
- `qualitative`: cloud growth or backlog attributed to AI in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3.
- `none`: the common answer, and the honest one for Meta and Amazon.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a named, located, sized capital commitment: a data-center campus with a site and a megawatt or gigawatt figure (Meta's Hyperion and Prometheus, Oracle's Abilene site, Microsoft's Fairwater), a power deal with a named plant or counterparty (Microsoft's Crane Clean Energy Center PPA), a joint venture or third-party financing for a named site (Meta's Louisiana venture: 20 percent owned, $27 billion estimated development cost, $45.95 billion maximum exposure), or a multi-year capacity commitment to a neocloud with an amount. Words that name one in releases and MD&A: "campus", "site", "broke ground", "gigawatt", "megawatts", "joint venture", "venture", "lease agreement", "commitment", "power purchase agreement", "maximum exposure to loss". Not a project: a model or product launch (Copilot, Gemini), a new chip generation, a hire, total-capex guidance with no site, a partnership with no amount.

## Traps

- A total-capex figure "to support our AI efforts" is the whole, never the AI part. Never copy it into `ai_amount`.
- Gross PP&E categories are cumulative balances; the flow is the difference between year-ends, and a disposal or reclassification can make it negative (then `none`).
- Meta's reported capex includes principal payments on finance leases ($72.22 billion for 2025 against $69.69 billion of purchases); `values.capex` is the purchases line. Say which one `basis` uses.
- Opex: AI shows up as depreciation of the fleet and as R&D headcount; no hyperscaler quantifies it. Expect `qualitative` or `none` for opex.
- A cloud segment (Intelligent Cloud, Google Cloud, AWS) is not AI revenue. An AI growth contribution in points is not a share of revenue. A run rate is not a year.
- Remaining performance obligations (Oracle $638 billion, Microsoft $678 billion) are contracted future revenue, not a project and not revenue in the year.
- Oracle's customer prepayments and customer-supplied GPUs ($75 billion) reduce Oracle's own capex; the GPUs the customer supplies are the customer's spend, not Oracle's.
- Leases not yet commenced are neither capex nor a liability yet; record the amount in `basis` as a forward signal, never in `ai_amount`.
- A capacity deal where the hyperscaler is the customer (Microsoft buying from CoreWeave, Meta's third-party cloud commitments) is a project for the hyperscaler and revenue for the seller; record who pays.

# Thesis: neocloud (neocloud@v3)

## Thesis

A neocloud is the pure play. The whole business is renting AI compute, so the whole capex is AI capex and the whole revenue is AI revenue. All four measures matter and all four are easy to read: capex allocation and revenue exposure are the whole business; projects are the GPU clusters, sites and customer contracts that the capex serves; plans versus reality is capex guidance against the actual, which moves with GPU deliveries and financing. The signal to watch is the gap between contracted backlog (customer commitments, purchase commitments for GPUs) and the capex the company can finance, because the balance sheet, not demand, is the constraint. The scale as of 2026: CoreWeave guides 2026 capex at $35 to $39 billion against a $104 billion backlog; Nebius guides $20 to $25 billion against more than $40 billion of customer commitments. Synergy Research puts the whole neocloud market above $25 billion of revenue in 2025, growing over 200% a year.

## Companies

CoreWeave (CRWV). The model neocloud and the reason the layer exists.
- Segment: none. The 10-Q for June 30 2026 says "The Company operates its business in one operating segment and, therefore, has one reportable segment." The FY2025 10-K reports the same single business.
- Revenue: $5,131 million in 2025, up from $1,915 million in 2024 (FY2025 release, Feb 26 2026). Q2 2026 revenue $2,575 million (Q2 2026 release, Aug 11 2026). All of it is AI cloud compute.
- Capex: "Purchase of property and equipment, including capitalized internal-use software" $10,309 million in 2025 (FY2025 release); the 10-K states cash paid for property and equipment of $10.3 billion in 2025 and $8.7 billion in 2024. Six months to June 30 2026: $14,117 million (10-Q). 2026 capex guidance $35 to $39 billion, given on the Q2 2026 call, not in the release (MarketBeat call highlights, Aug 11 2026).
- Stated AI share of capex or revenue: none stated, and none needed; the filings describe one business, AI cloud. Not disclosed as a share as of 2026-10-29 (FY2025 10-K, Q2 2026 10-Q checked).
- Backlog: revenue backlog $66.8 billion at Dec 31 2025 and about $104 billion at June 30 2026; defined as "remaining performance obligations, plus other amounts we estimate will be recognized as revenue in future periods" under committed contracts. RPO $60.7 billion at Dec 31 2025 (up 302% from $15.1 billion) and $103.7 billion at June 30 2026.
- Customers: Microsoft was "approximately 67% of our revenue" in 2025 (10-K); the top two customers were about 77% in 2024. In Q2 2026 Customer A was 36%, Customer B 26%, Customer C 10% of revenue (10-Q). OpenAI "has committed to pay us up to approximately $11.9 billion through October 2030" plus "up to approximately $6.5 billion through May 31, 2031"; Meta "initially committed to pay us up to approximately $14.2 billion through December 2031" (10-K).
- Financing: total indebtedness $21.6 billion at Dec 31 2025; DDTL 1.0 up to $2.3 billion, DDTL 2.0 up to $7.6 billion, DDTL 2.1 up to $3.0 billion, DDTL 3.0 up to $2.6 billion; $2.0 billion 2030 notes, $1.75 billion 2031 notes, $2.6 billion 1.75% convertible notes due 2031 (10-K). At June 30 2026: recourse debt $31,405 million, non-recourse debt $3,663 million, finance lease liabilities $221 million (Q2 2026 release and 10-Q). Operating lease liabilities $8.2 billion at Dec 31 2025.
- Power: over 850 MW active and about 3.1 GW contracted at Dec 31 2025; 1.5 GW active and about 3.7 GW contracted at June 30 2026; 43 data centers at year end 2025. All GPUs are NVIDIA GPUs (10-K).

Nebius Group (NBIS). The second pure play, at the edge of the layer because of its other businesses and its filing form.
- Segments: three, named "Nebius", "Avride" and "TripleTen" in the FY2025 annual report. Segment revenue 2025 (2024): Nebius $480.3 million ($68.3 million), Avride $1.3 million ($0.3 million), TripleTen $54.1 million ($28.8 million); total revenue $529.8 million ($91.5 million). The Nebius segment is the AI cloud. Toloka was deconsolidated in May 2025; ClickHouse and Toloka are equity stakes. In 2026 letters the company reports "Nebius AI cloud" against "Other businesses".
- AI share: the Nebius segment was 91% of 2025 revenue (computed from the segment table above). Q1 2026: Nebius AI revenue $390 million of $399 million group revenue, "98% of group revenue" (Q1 2026 call). Q2 2026: $574.9 million of $582.3 million, about 98% (Q2 2026 letter). ARR $3.0 billion at end of June 2026.
- Capex: purchases of property and equipment $4,066.0 million in 2025 and $807.5 million in 2024 (FY2025 20-F). Q2 2026 capex about $5.7 billion, "mostly for GPUs, GPU-related hardware, and data center expansion." 2026 capex guidance raised to $20 to $25 billion from $16 to $20 billion (Q1 2026 call, May 13 2026) and held in Q2.
- Contracts: Microsoft, signed Sept 8 2025, "total contract value is about $17.4 billion through 2031," up to about $19.4 billion with optional capacity, served from Vineland, New Jersey (6-K). Meta, Nov 2025, "approximately $3 billion, with a five-year term" (Q3 2025 letter). Meta, signed March 13 2026, "up to approximately $27 billion": $12 billion of dedicated GPU clusters from early 2027 plus an unsold-capacity order of up to $15 billion (6-K). Customer commitments "more than $40 billion" at Q2 2026; customer prepayments expected above $9 billion in 2026.
- Customer concentration: no percentages disclosed as of 2026-10-29 (FY2025 20-F and Q2 2026 letter checked).
- Power: about 170 MW active at Dec 31 2025; more than 2 GW contracted by Feb 2026; 5 GW contracted expected by end of 2026.
- Filing form: Nebius filed a Form 20-F for FY2025 and says it expects to keep foreign private issuer status, so the 10-K pipeline holds no annual report for it yet; its years are gaps until a 10-K exists.

Miners that host GPUs (IREN, Applied Digital, Core Scientific, which Synergy lists among neoclouds) look like neoclouds but keep a mining segment; they sit in `miner_to_hpc`.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Capex** (`values.capex`) is almost entirely GPUs, servers, networking and datacenter fit-out. CoreWeave's 10-K says capital investments "consist primarily of servers and network equipment for computing, storage, and networking requirements." Nebius says Q2 2026 capex was "mostly for GPUs, GPU-related hardware, and data center expansion."
2. **Finance leases** (`facts.finance_lease_liability`) and GPU-backed debt carry part of the buildout outside cash capex. At CoreWeave the finance leases are small ($221 million at June 30 2026); the DDTL facilities and non-recourse debt ($3.7 billion) are the GPU-backed part, and operating leases ($8.2 billion of liabilities) carry the shells.
3. **Purchase commitments** (`facts.purchase_commitments`): contracted GPU deliveries and datacenter capacity. CoreWeave's 10-K refers to lease commitments not yet commenced and enforceable purchase commitments (Note 9); amounts were not in the fetched text as of 2026-10-29.
4. **Revenue and backlog** (`values.revenue`, `ai_spend`): all revenue is AI compute; contracted backlog with named customers is the forward number. CoreWeave: RPO and revenue backlog. Nebius: customer commitments and ARR.
5. **Customer prepayments** (deferred revenue): CoreWeave's deferred revenue was $9.7 billion at June 30 2026; Nebius expects over $9 billion of prepayments in 2026. Prepayments fund capex before revenue arrives.

## How to attribute

Capex:

- `stated_amount` or `stated_share` when the company gives one. Neither company has given an AI share of capex as of 2026-10-29, because the whole of it is AI. Otherwise:
- `whole_business`: `ai_amount = capex`, confidence 0.9, `basis` "a single-segment AI cloud: all capex is AI infrastructure". Cite `values.capex` for the year. CoreWeave: cite the one-segment statement. Nebius: confidence ≤ 0.7 while Avride and TripleTen sit in consolidated capex (they were 9% of 2025 revenue), or `segment` when the company reports the Nebius segment's capex. The FY2025 20-F gives segment revenue, not segment capex; check the segment note of each later filing.

Opex: cost of revenue is running the fleet (power, depreciation, datacenter leases); `whole_business` with confidence 0.7 for opex is defensible; say so. CoreWeave's cost of revenue rose 181% year on year in Q2 2026 (10-Q), tracking the fleet.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share` / `stated_amount`: rarely needed; the company does not split what is all one thing. Nebius does state the AI cloud share ("98% of group revenue" in Q1 and Q2 2026); use it with confidence ≤ 0.9.
- `segment`: Nebius, the "Nebius" segment's revenue ($480.3 million in 2025) separately from Avride and TripleTen; confidence ≤ 0.8.

## Projects

A project is a GPU cluster or site with a size and a counterparty: a data-center lease or build with megawatts and a location (Nebius's Vineland, New Jersey site for Microsoft; its 1.2 GW owned Pennsylvania site), a GPU delivery contract with a count or an amount, a customer contract with a named customer and amount (CoreWeave's contracts with Microsoft, OpenAI up to $11.9 billion plus $6.5 billion, and Meta up to $14.2 billion; Nebius's Microsoft $17.4 billion and Meta $3 billion and $27 billion contracts), and a financing facility tied to a named site or GPU batch (CoreWeave's DDTL facilities; Nebius's $775 million secured facility backed by deployed GPUs). Not a project: general availability of a new GPU type, a software feature, a hire, an equity raise with no use named.

# Thesis: bitcoin miner turned HPC / AI host (miner_to_hpc@v3)

## Thesis

These companies own cheap power and sites, and they are turning them from bitcoin mining into GPU hosting or AI cloud. Two businesses share one balance sheet, and only the HPC or AI segment is AI spend. Capex allocation (segment capex), revenue exposure (segment revenue) and project-level investment (a named campus converted under a lease with a hyperscaler or neocloud) all matter; plans versus reality matters because HPC capex guidance is large relative to the company and often slips. The signal to watch is the HPC segment's capex against its revenue, year by year: it shows whether the conversion is earning yet, and the mining segment is noise.

The facts as of 29 Oct 2026 show how far apart the two numbers sit. Applied Digital spent $2,988.7m of capex on its HPC Hosting segment in fiscal 2026 against $385.3m of segment revenue. IREN spent $4.3bn on plant, equipment and computer hardware in fiscal 2026 against $128.8m of AI Cloud revenue, with $13.8bn of capex commitments due within a year. The leases behind the capex are long and large ($7.0bn to $12.8bn per company over 10 to 25 years) and are usually backstopped by Google, so the contract value, not the revenue, is what the market prices. Both numbers belong in the dataset, in different fields.

1. **Segment capex** (`facts.segment_capex`, ASC 280) is the hard number: the HPC / AI cloud / colocation segment's capital expenditures. Applied Digital is the one company that reports it (HPC Hosting $2,988.7m in fiscal 2026). IREN, Core Scientific, TeraWulf, Hut 8 and Galaxy report segment revenue but consolidated capex only.
2. **Segment revenue** (`facts.segment_revenue`) for the same segment shows whether the capex is already earning: IREN "AI Cloud", Applied Digital "HPC Hosting Business", Core Scientific "Colocation", TeraWulf "HPC Leasing", Galaxy "Data Centers", Bit Digital "cloud services" and "colocation services", Soluna "High-Performance Computing Services".
3. **What the company says** (`ai_spend`): GPU purchases with counts and amounts (Bit Digital's 130 H200 servers for about $30m), per-MW build costs (Cipher's $9m to $11m per critical IT MW), capex guidance (IREN's $25bn to $30bn for fiscal 2027), capex commitments (IREN's $13.8bn at 30 June 2026).

## How to attribute

Capex, in order of hardness:

- `segment`: `ai_amount = segment capex` of the AI/HPC segment(s) for the year. If several segments are AI/HPC (hosting plus cloud), add them and list every fact used. As of the FY2025/FY2026 filings this works for Applied Digital only.
- `stated_amount`: an explicit AI amount from a filing or release when no segment capex exists for that year (a GPU purchase with a dollar figure, a stated HPC build spend).
- `ppe_category`: growth in a GPU/HPC-specific PP&E category, when the note separates it.
- `qualitative`: consolidated capex said to be mostly HPC (TeraWulf's $1.06bn in 2025, Galaxy's $1.19bn in 2025) with no segment split: no amount, confidence ≤ 0.3, name the consolidated figure in `basis`.
- `none` otherwise, including every year a company reports mining only (Cipher through 2025, Riot, MARA, CleanSpark).

Opex: `segment` cost of revenue for the AI segment when the filing states it (IREN AI Cloud cost of revenue $16.9m in fiscal 2026, TeraWulf HPC Leasing cost of revenue $2.5m in 2025); otherwise `none`.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_amount` / `stated_share`: when the company states HPC or AI revenue for the year outside the segment note; confidence ≤ 0.9. Bitdeer's AI cloud revenue of $6.8m in 2025 is this kind.
- `segment`: sum of the `segment_revenue` facts for the HPC / AI segment(s): IREN "AI Cloud", Applied Digital "HPC Hosting Business", Core Scientific "Colocation", TeraWulf "HPC Leasing", Galaxy "Data Centers", Bit Digital "cloud services" plus "colocation services", Soluna "High-Performance Computing Services". Name every segment used. Confidence ≤ 0.8. Colocation revenue from a hyperscaler or neocloud tenant counts: the lease is AI hosting even though the GPUs are the tenant's.
- `qualitative`: the company links revenue growth to HPC in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3.
- `none`: a year with only mining revenue, or with a segment total and no HPC line. Hut 8's Compute segment is mining plus AI cloud with no split: `none`, with the segment named in `basis`. MARA's hosting services line is miner hosting: `none`. Soluna's Data Center Hosting is bitcoin hosting: `none`.
- `whole_business`: never; the mining segment is always there.

## Projects

A project is a named site converted or built for HPC with a counterparty, megawatts or an amount: a campus lease with a hyperscaler or neocloud (Applied Digital's Polaris Forge 1 at Ellendale leased to CoreWeave, 400 MW, about $11.0bn; Core Scientific's sites contracted to CoreWeave, about 590 MW; TeraWulf's Lake Mariner and Abernathy leased to Fluidstack, 522 MW, over $12.8bn; Cipher's Barber Lake to Fluidstack and Black Pearl to AWS, 600 MW; Hut 8's River Bend to Fluidstack, 245 MW, $7.0bn; Galaxy's Helios to CoreWeave, 800 MW; IREN's Horizon at Childress for Microsoft, $9.7bn; Riot's Rockdale lease to AMD, 25 MW), a GPU purchase with a count and amount, a financing tied to a site (Galaxy's $1.4bn Helios facility, Cipher's senior secured notes for Barber Lake), a joint venture with a stake and a site (TeraWulf's 50.1% of Abernathy, MARA's Starwood venture). Words that name one: "campus", "lease", "critical IT load", "megawatts", "gigawatt", "hosting agreement", "GPUs", "energized", "phase", "backstop", "rent commencement". Not a project: a hashrate target, an ASIC purchase, a mining site expansion, a new power contract with no HPC use, a hire.

## Traps

- Mining capex (ASICs, "miners", "mining equipment", "deposits on equipment" for miners) is not AI. Never include the mining segment. Riot paid about $228.4m for miners in 2025; none of it is AI.
- Colocation shells leased to a hyperscaler are AI infrastructure spend by this company even though the GPUs are the tenant's; count the segment capex, say in `basis` that the GPUs are the tenant's. When the tenant funds the build (CoreWeave at Core Scientific), say so; the capex is still this company's.
- A year with a segment total but no AI segment line (before the pivot) is `none`, not zero. Cipher, Riot, MARA and CleanSpark are `none` for 2025 with large project rows.
- A lease's total contract value ("$7.0 billion over 15 years", "over $12.8 billion") is a project amount, not revenue in the year. Contracted ARR (IREN's $4bn) is a run-rate, not a fiscal-year figure.
- Bitcoin price lifts mining revenue and total revenue together; only the HPC segment is attributable.
- A segment that mixes mining and AI cloud (Hut 8's Compute) cannot be attributed by segment; wait for the split.
- Hosting revenue is usually miner hosting (MARA, Soluna's Data Center Hosting, Applied Digital's Data Center Hosting Business), not AI hosting; read the segment definition before counting it.
- A per-MW cost estimate times contracted MW is a reader's calculation, not a stated amount; it goes in `basis`, not `ai_amount`.
- Bitdeer files 20-F; its years are a gap for the pipeline. Bit Digital's cloud business sits in a consolidated subsidiary (WhiteFiber) with its own filings; use Bit Digital's segment, not WhiteFiber's.

# Thesis: chip seller (chip_seller@v3)

## Thesis

Chip sellers are paid by the buildout. Revenue exposure is the measure that matters: the data-center or AI line of revenue is the hyperscalers' capex arriving. Capex allocation does not matter here, with one exception, Intel, whose capex is fabs and mostly not AI either. Project-level investment matters where a seller builds a fab or commits capital to a customer or partner (Nvidia's investments in Intel, Groq and OpenAI, Intel's fabs), and plans versus reality matters only for Intel's capex guidance. The signal to watch is the data-center revenue line and its growth, read against the hyperscalers' capex in the same period. The scale as of the latest filings: Nvidia's Data Center line was $193.7 billion in fiscal 2026 (year to January 25, 2026), up 68%; AMD's Data Center segment $16.6 billion in 2025, up 32%; Marvell's data center end market $6.1 billion in fiscal 2026, up 46%; Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue grew 74% in its fourth quarter of fiscal 2025. TrendForce put Nvidia at about 70% of the AI chip market in 2025 and expects custom ASIC shipments to pass GPU shipments by 2026, which is why the custom-silicon sellers (Broadcom, Marvell) sit here with Nvidia.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Segment or market revenue** (`facts.segment_revenue`): the data-center or AI line. Nvidia "Data Center" (revenue by market platform), AMD "Data Center" segment, Broadcom "Semiconductor solutions" (AI semiconductor revenue is stated in releases and calls), Marvell "Data center" end market, Intel "Data Center and AI", Monolithic Power "Enterprise Data", Texas Instruments "Data center" (call only). This is the seller side of the buyers' capex: what hyperscalers paid them.
2. **Their own capex** (`values.capex`) is not AI spend in the ledger's sense. Nvidia's was $6.1 billion against $193.7 billion of Data Center revenue. Intel's fabs are the exception that proves it: $17.7 billion gross capex, mostly not AI.
3. **What the company says** (`ai_spend`): AI revenue figures (Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue, TI's data center line), AI-attributed R&D, and capital commitments to counterparties (Nvidia's $17.5 billion of private investments, $13 billion Groq licence, $5 billion Intel stake, pending OpenAI agreement).
4. **Customer concentration** is a reliability signal, not an input: Astera Labs one customer over 70%; Credo top 10 about 90%; Broadcom top five end customers about 40%.

## How to attribute

Capex:

- `none` unless the company states an AI amount or share of its own capex (rare: a GPU cluster for internal AI research, Nvidia's "DGX Cloud"). Say in `basis` that a chip seller's capex funds fabs and test, not AI infrastructure.

Opex:

- `stated_share` or `stated_amount` only; otherwise `qualitative` when R&D is said to be AI-driven, else `none`.

Record the seller-side signal in `basis` as before: the data-center segment revenue for the year, cited, so the attribution shows what was received from AI buyers even when nothing is attributed. The revenue field below is where that signal becomes a row.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share`: the company states AI's share of revenue; confidence ≤ 0.9. None of Astera Labs, Credo, SiTime or Rambus states one as of 2026-10-29; do not invent one from a product description.
- `stated_amount`: the company states AI revenue for the year. Broadcom states "AI semiconductor revenue" in releases and on calls; use it rather than the Semiconductor solutions segment, which includes non-AI chips. Confidence ≤ 0.9 when the amount is in a release or filing, ≤ 0.6 when it is only in call coverage. Texas Instruments' data center line (call, not 10-K): ≤ 0.7.
- `segment`: sum of the `segment_revenue` facts that are the data-center line. Nvidia "Data Center" (the market line, not the "Compute & Networking" segment), AMD "Data Center" segment, Marvell "Data center" end market: confidence ≤ 0.8, with `basis` noting that the line includes non-AI servers (AMD's includes EPYC CPUs). Intel "Data Center and AI" is mostly general-purpose Xeon: confidence ≤ 0.5 and say so. Monolithic Power "Enterprise Data": ≤ 0.6.
- `qualitative`: revenue growth attributed to AI in words only (Qualcomm, Rambus, SiTime, Arm, Credo, Astera Labs), confidence ≤ 0.3.
- `none`: Synopsys and Cadence, and any seller with no AI or data-center line; the honest answer for a design-tool vendor whose customers build AI chips.
- `whole_business`: never, even for Astera Labs or Credo; use what they state.

## Projects

A project is a fab, a packaging or test site, or a capital commitment to a named counterparty with an amount: Intel's fabs (Arizona and Oregon 18A ramp, Ohio) and the government's equity stake, Nvidia's $5 billion Intel stake, its $13 billion Groq licence and its pending OpenAI agreement, a supercomputer the company builds for itself. Words that name one: "fab", "wafer", "investment of up to", "letter of intent", "equity investment", "capacity", "campus", "gigawatts" when the seller commits to supply or fund them. Not a project: a product launch (a new GPU or accelerator generation), a design win, a supply agreement with no capital from this company, a hire.

## Traps

- Data-center revenue is not this company's AI spend. It is the buyers' spend arriving. Never put it in `ai_amount` for capex; it belongs in the revenue field.
- "Compute & Networking" (Nvidia's segment, $193,479 million in fiscal 2026) includes automotive and professional visualization; the market line "Data Center" ($193.7 billion) is the AI one. The two are close in size but not the same fact.
- Broadcom's Semiconductor solutions segment ($36,858 million) is not AI revenue; the stated AI semiconductor figure is.
- Intel's Data Center and AI segment is a data-center line, not an AI one; cap the confidence.
- A supply commitment from a customer (gigawatts of GPUs to be delivered) is the customer's project; for the seller it is backlog, not spend. Nvidia's $95.2 billion of inventory purchase and supply obligations (10-K) is its own commitment to foundries, not AI capex.
- Nvidia's $17.5 billion of private investments and the $13 billion Groq payment are investing cash flows, not capex; record them as projects with the counterparty, never in `ai_amount`.
- A "data center" end market that appears only on a call (Texas Instruments) is not in the segment note; cite the call and cap the confidence.
- Marvell consolidated its non-data-center end markets into "Communications and other" in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026; older enterprise networking and carrier facts are not comparable to the new line.

# Thesis: memory, storage, networking, optics and servers (component_supplier@v3)

## Thesis

These companies sell the parts and boxes around the GPU: memory, drives, switches, optics, servers and the contract manufacturing that assembles them. They are paid by the buildout, so revenue exposure is the measure that matters. Capex allocation matters for one company, Micron, whose fab and HBM capacity is the one supplier capex that is partly AI and said to be: Micron spent $30.7 billion gross ($27.4 billion net of incentives) in fiscal 2026 and guides about $25 billion net for the first half of fiscal 2027 alone, "higher in the second half". Project-level investment matters for the fab builders (Micron) and the factory builders (Supermicro, Dell, the contract manufacturers); plans versus reality matters for Micron's capex guidance. The signal to watch is the data-center or AI line of revenue where the company names one (Dell's AI-optimized servers, Sandisk's Datacenter, Coherent's Datacenter & Communications, Fabrinet's Data center, Cisco's hyperscaler AI orders) and the capex Micron commits to HBM and DRAM.

## How to attribute

Capex and opex:

- Micron: `stated_share` or `stated_amount` if the company gives the HBM or AI share of capex; it has not, as of the fiscal 2026 10-K. Otherwise `qualitative` with confidence ≤ 0.4 ("capex to support HBM- and DRAM-related investments").
- Arista, Cisco: `none` for capex (their capex is small and not AI); `qualitative` or `none` for opex.
- Coherent: `qualitative` ≤ 0.4 for capex while the expansion is stated as indium phosphide for AI datacenters with no amount split.
- Every other company here: `none` for capex unless an expansion is stated as being for AI demand with an amount; `qualitative` or `none` for opex.
- As with chip sellers, record data-center or AI revenue in `basis` as the seller-side signal, never in `ai_amount`; the revenue field below is where it becomes a row.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share`: the company states AI's share of revenue. Supermicro states the share from AI solutions on calls (about 60% in Q4 fiscal 2026); use it. Confidence ≤ 0.9 for a filing, ≤ 0.7 for a call figure.
- `stated_amount`: the company states AI revenue for the year: Dell's AI-optimized server revenue ($24.7 billion fiscal 2026), Cisco's hyperscaler AI infrastructure revenue (about $4 billion fiscal 2026), Jabil's AI-related revenue ($14.4 billion fiscal 2026, call). Orders and backlog are not revenue: confidence ≤ 0.5 for an orders figure (Dell's $64 billion, HPE's $6.8 billion, Cisco's $9.3 billion) and say so. Confidence ≤ 0.9 for a revenue figure in a release, ≤ 0.7 from a call.
- `segment`: sum of the `segment_revenue` facts that are the data-center line, named per company. Micron CMBU from fiscal 2025 (before that "Compute and Networking", which includes client and graphics; ≤ 0.5); CDBU is data center too but includes enterprise storage and non-AI DRAM, ≤ 0.5. Sandisk Datacenter, AAOI Datacenter, Fabrinet Data center: ≤ 0.6. Coherent Datacenter & Communications: ≤ 0.5 (communications is telecom). Dell "Infrastructure Solutions Group" and HPE "Server" are data-center lines that include non-AI servers: ≤ 0.5. Celestica CCS or HPS, Jabil Intelligent Infrastructure, Flex Cloud and Power Infrastructure, Penguin Advanced Computing: ≤ 0.6. Arista and Cisco have no AI segment; do not use "Product" or "Networking" as one. Lumentum has no segment since fiscal 2026; Components and Systems are product lines, not markets.
- `qualitative`: revenue growth attributed to AI or cloud demand in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3. The answer for Western Digital, Seagate, NetApp and Ciena (cloud provider share is a customer mix, not an AI line).
- `none`: no link stated.
- `whole_business`: never, even for Supermicro; use its stated share.

## Projects

A project is a fab or factory with a location and an amount: Micron's fabs (Idaho, New York, Singapore, Japan) and HBM packaging capacity, Supermicro's and Dell's plant expansions, Coherent's indium phosphide capacity, a contract manufacturer's new site stated as being for AI or data-center customers. Words that name one: "fab", "facility", "campus", "expansion", "investment of", "capacity", "square feet" with a location. Not a project: a product launch (a new drive, switch or server), a customer win, an order figure, a spin-off, a hire.

## Traps

- A memory upcycle lifts total revenue; only the AI/HBM part is attributable, and only when stated. Micron's fiscal 2026 revenue more than tripled; the 10-K gives a data-center share (about 60%), not an AI one.
- Orders, bookings and backlog are not revenue; a stated AI order figure gets a low ceiling and the word "orders" in `basis`. Cisco states both orders ($9.3 billion) and revenue (about $4 billion) for the same year; take the revenue.
- A server segment (Dell ISG, HPE Server) is a data-center line, not an AI one; cap the confidence. Dell's AI-optimized servers line is the AI one.
- Micron renamed its segments in fiscal 2025; an older "Compute and Networking" fact is not comparable to "Cloud Memory".
- A call figure (Supermicro's 60%, Jabil's $14.4 billion, Arista's 48% titans) is not in the filing; cite the call and cap the confidence.
- Cloud end markets (Western Digital's almost 90%, Ciena's 53%) are customer groups, not AI lines.

# Thesis: adopters, physical AI and commodities (other@v3)

## Thesis

This layer holds the companies that fit no other model: adopters that buy AI as a cost line, physical AI (robots, vehicles, rockets) and the commodity and network end of the chain. There is no industry pattern to lean on, so only what the company states counts. Capex allocation matters where stated: SpaceX states AI capex by segment ($15.8 billion in Q2 2026), Tesla guides total capex and names AI as a use without an AI amount. Project-level investment matters where a company names a cluster, plant or investment program (Tesla's Cortex, Apple's Houston server plant, ExxonMobil's data-center gas plant); revenue exposure matters only for the physical-AI sellers and is qualitative; plans versus reality applies only where the company guides AI spend (Tesla's 2026 capex cut from over $25 billion to about $20 billion). The signal to watch is a stated AI amount, and its absence: for most companies here the honest answer is `none`.

## How to attribute

Capex and opex:

- `segment`: SpaceX's AI segment capex ($15.8 billion in Q2 2026), with `basis` naming the segment and that it is a cloud and model business, not Tesla-style adoption.
- `stated_amount` / `stated_share`: only what the company states as the AI part (`scope: ai`). Tesla states it when a release gives an AI-related capex line; use it when present, and record "not disclosed" when the period's release does not.
- `qualitative` when spend is linked to AI in words only (Tesla's 2026 guidance, Walmart's technology capex, JPMorgan's technology budget); `none` otherwise.
- Never estimate from PP&E categories or segments here: there is no industry pattern to lean on, and a guess would be a number with nothing behind it.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `segment`: SpaceX's AI segment revenue ($2.56 billion in Q2 2026), confidence ≤ 0.7, `basis` "AI cloud and model revenue, segment as reported". Not allowed for anyone else: IBM's Software and Consulting, the carriers' wireless, Freeport's regions and Compass's brokerage are not AI lines.
- `stated_amount` / `stated_share`: only when the company states AI revenue or AI's share of revenue; confidence ≤ 0.8. Rare; IBM's $12.5 billion gen-AI book of business is cumulative bookings, not revenue, ≤ 0.4 and only when a release or filing states it.
- `qualitative`: revenue linked to AI or data-center demand in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3. Symbotic (warehouse automation is the product), Freeport (copper demand from data centers when the company says so, as in its January 2026 deck), the carriers (fiber to data centers when stated).
- `none`: the common answer for adopters.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a stated, sized AI investment with a site or a program: Tesla's Cortex training clusters (over 90 MW and over 115 MW, ramping to about 400 MW at Giga Texas) and the plants it ties to AI and robotics, SpaceX's Colossus data centers and the Anthropic cloud agreement ($1.25 billion a month through May 2029), Apple's Houston server plant and $600 billion US program, an ExxonMobil power project once it has a size, a bank's or retailer's named AI data center when stated with an amount. Words that name one: "cluster", "GPUs", "training compute", "megawatts", "data center", "cloud services agreement", "invest $" with a term, "facility" with a location and an AI use. Not a project: a product launch (a phone, a robot, a model), a technology budget total, a fiber or spectrum build, a mine expansion with no AI link, an acquisition, a hire.

## Traps

- "Technology" or "software" capex is not AI capex (Walmart, JPMorgan, Compass).
- Opex: AI headcount, token or model costs are rarely quantified (Uber's AI budget has no public number); `none` is the common, honest answer.
- A carrier's fiber build serves data centers among many customers; it is network capex, not AI, unless the company states an AI part.
- Copper or robot revenue is physical-end exposure in words only; never make it a share without a statement.
- A guidance cut (Tesla, over $25 billion to about $20 billion) with no program breakdown says nothing about the AI part; record the total and the absence.
- A national investment pledge (Apple's $600 billion over four years) is a program total across many uses, not AI capex; only the named AI server plant is a project, and its cost is not disclosed.
- SpaceX's AI segment is the exception that proves the rule: when a company here reports an AI segment, use `segment`; when it does not, do not build one.

# Thesis: chip equipment and materials (chip_equipment@v3)

## Thesis

Equipment makers are one step upstream of the chips. They are paid by foundry and memory capex, which is itself pulled by AI demand for leading-edge logic, HBM and advanced packaging. SEMI put 300mm fab equipment spending at $133 billion for 2026 (up 18 percent) and $151 billion for 2027, and credited AI chip demand and HBM (SEMI, 1 Apr 2026). Revenue exposure is the measure that matters, and it is only as good as what the company states, because end-market lines (foundry, memory, DRAM) are broader than AI. Capex allocation does not matter: their own capex is tool factories, labs and R&D sites, and none of the eight states an AI part of it. Project-level investment matters a little (plant and R&D expansions); plans versus reality does not. The signal to watch is the stated AI, HBM or advanced-packaging share or amount of revenue, and behind it the capex of TSMC, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix, which the ledger does not hold. TrendForce put DRAM makers' capex at $53.7 billion for 2025 and $61.3 billion for 2026, aimed at HBM and process upgrades rather than new capacity (TechNews citing TrendForce, 14 Nov 2025).

Teradyne's approximately 70 percent (Q1 2026) is the example; Onto's "nearly half" from advanced packaging and specialty devices is a share of a broader line, ≤ 0.5.
- `stated_amount`: the company states AI-related or advanced-packaging revenue for the year; confidence ≤ 0.8. KLA's about $1.1 billion of advanced-packaging process-control revenue for calendar 2026 is an outlook figure, ≤ 0.5 until reported.
- `segment`: not allowed for "Foundry", "Memory", "DRAM", "Systems", "Semiconductor Systems", "Semiconductor Process Control" or "Semiconductor Test"; they are end markets broader than AI, and a DRAM line is not an HBM line. Record them in `basis` only. One exception: Advanced Energy's "Data Center Computing" is a product line sold to hyperscalers for AI servers; `segment` with confidence ≤ 0.6, with `basis` noting it includes non-AI server power.
- `qualitative`: AI named as the driver of demand with no figure, confidence ≤ 0.3. The answer for Lam, Entegris and Axcelis as of 2026-10-29.
- `none`: no link stated.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a plant or R&D site expansion with a location and an amount: a new tool factory (Advanced Energy's Thailand factory), a research center, a packaging-development line. Words that name one: "facility", "campus", "expansion", "square feet", "investment of", "center" with a location. Not a project: a tool launch (Applied's six new DRAM and packaging systems), a customer's fab (the customer's project, not this company's), an order, a hire, a merger.

## Traps

- "AI drove N% of our revenue" is a demand statement, not the company's spend. It belongs in `basis` for capex and in the revenue field as `stated_share`.
- Equipment capex cycles follow the foundries and memory makers, not this company's AI decisions.
- A share of orders, shipments or backlog is not a share of revenue; cap the confidence and say which it was. Onto's backlog above $1.1 billion is backlog.
- A growth rate ("advanced packaging up more than 70 percent") is not a share or an amount; it belongs in `basis` unless the base amount is also stated.
- A customer's fab announcement (TSMC Arizona, Micron Idaho) is not this company's project.
- Applied's DRAM share of Semiconductor Systems (26 percent in Q3 FY2026) is a DRAM line; HBM is part of it, not all of it.
- Advanced Energy's data-center line is the one place in this layer where `segment` is allowed; do not extend that to its Semiconductor Equipment line.

# Thesis: data-center build suppliers (datacenter_build@v3)

## Thesis

These companies turn a hyperscaler's capex into a building: power distribution, cooling, switchgear, turbines, fuel cells and the construction labour. They are paid by the buildout, so revenue exposure (data-center revenue and backlog) is the measure that matters. Capex allocation rarely matters: their capex is factories and fleets, attributable only when an expansion is tied to data-center demand with a number. Project-level investment matters for those plant expansions and for named construction contracts; plans versus reality does not. The signal to watch is the data-center share of orders and backlog, which runs a year or more ahead of revenue. In mid-2026 that signal was loud: GE Vernova's data-center orders passed $5 billion year to date by July, more than double all of 2025; Eaton's Electrical Americas backlog was up 33%; Powell booked a single data-center order above $400 million; Modine signed a $4 billion chiller agreement with one hyperscaler.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Segment revenue and backlog** (`facts.segment_revenue`, `ai_spend`): "Data center" as an end market or vertical; backlog or orders tied to data centers ("data center orders", "mega order", "slot reservation"); "hyperscale" in releases.
2. **What the company says** (`ai_spend`): capacity expansions explicitly for data-center demand ("liquid-cooling manufacturing expansion", "capex tied to Data Centers growth", "Jacintoport fabrication yard expansion").
3. **Capex** (`values.capex`): factory capacity. AI spend only when the company ties an expansion to data-center demand and gives a number; in 2026 none of the eleven did in a release.

## How to attribute

Capex and opex:

- `stated_amount` / `stated_share` when the company states a capex amount or share for data-center capacity (`scope: ai` or `scope: datacenter`).
- `qualitative` with confidence ≤ 0.4 when capex is linked to data-center demand in words only (Modine, nVent, Powell in 2026).
- `none` otherwise. Data-center revenue or backlog goes in `basis`, never in `ai_amount`; the revenue field below is where it becomes a row.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share`: the company states the data-center share of revenue. As of 29 October 2026 none of the eleven stated one in a release; shares in call coverage (JCI high teens, Quanta 15 to 20%, Powell about 15% of backlog) are call statements, confidence ≤ 0.5, and `basis` must say "call, not release or filing". Data center is broader than AI: confidence ≤ 0.7 at best and say "data center, not AI" in `basis`.
- `stated_amount`: the company states data-center revenue or orders for the period (GE Vernova's $5 billion of data-center orders, Modine's $4 billion chiller agreement, Powell's $400 million order); confidence ≤ 0.7 for revenue. An orders, agreement or backlog figure is not revenue: ≤ 0.4.
- `segment`: only where a reported segment is the data-center line. Modine's Data Centers group once it reports as a segment; nVent's Systems Protection is data-center heavy but not a data-center segment. Vertiv's regions, Eaton's Electrical Americas, JCI's regions, Quanta's Electric, EMCOR's electrical construction and GE Vernova's Power are not data-center lines; do not sum them. Confidence ≤ 0.6.
- `qualitative`: data-center demand named as a driver with no figure, confidence ≤ 0.3. The 2026 answer for Vertiv, Eaton, JCI, Quanta, EMCOR, Comfort and Bloom from their releases.
- `none`: no link stated (Comfort Systems' Q2 2026 release).
- `whole_business`: never, even for Vertiv; use a stated share when one appears.

## Projects

A project is a plant or capacity expansion the company ties to data-center demand with a location and an amount, or a named data-center construction, equipment or turbine contract with a size: a new switchgear or cooling plant, added turbine capacity, a contracted campus build with megawatts, a multi-year supply agreement with a hyperscaler. Words that name one: "facility", "plant", "expansion", "capacity", "investment of", "contract", "agreement", "mega order", "slot reservation", "megawatts", "gigawatts" with a site or a customer. Not a project: a new product (a cooling unit, a turbine model), an order-growth statement, backlog totals, a hire.

Named as of 29 October 2026: Modine's $4 billion hyperscale chiller agreement; Powell's $400 million-plus behind-the-meter data-center order and Jacintoport expansion; nVent's liquid-cooling plant expansion; GE Vernova's 116 GW of gas backlog and slot reservations and $6 billion 2025 to 2028 capex program (not data-center specific).

## Traps

- Data-center revenue is the customer's spend, not this company's.
- Construction firms (Quanta, Comfort Systems, EMCOR) have small capex; their AI exposure is revenue mix. Expect `none` with a strong `basis`.
- Data center is not AI; every revenue ceiling here is capped for that reason.
- Orders, agreements, slot reservations and backlog run ahead of revenue; never sum them into a revenue row. GE Vernova's slot reservations are not even firm orders.
- A turbine or switchgear plant built for all customers is a project only when the company ties it to data-center demand.
- Numbers in call summaries (Vertiv backlog, nVent data-center sales, Eaton data-center growth, JCI share) are not in the releases; cite the call or leave the field at the release's ceiling.

# Thesis: data-center landlord (datacenter_landlord@v3)

## Thesis

Landlords build shells and lease power and space to hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises. Their capex is data-center capacity, which is broader than AI, so capex allocation matters but is capped: development capex is the number, and AI's part of it is rarely stated. Project-level investment matters most: campuses, megawatts under construction, joint ventures and hyperscale leases are where the AI link is visible. Plans versus reality matters for development capex guidance, and in 2026 the guidance moved a lot: Equinix raised 2026 capex from $3.655 to 4.155 billion (February) to $5.0 to 6.0 billion (July); Digital Realty raised 2026 development capex from $3.5 to 4.0 billion (April) to $4.25 to 4.75 billion (July). Revenue exposure matters least: rent is rent, and no segment is the AI one. The signal to watch is megawatts under construction and pre-leased, the backlog of signed-but-not-commenced rent, and the share of development funded off balance sheet through joint ventures.

## Companies

Equinix (EQIX), Digital Realty (DLR) and Iron Mountain (IRM). Equinix and Digital Realty are data-center REITs through and through; Digital Realty's hyperscale development is the closer to AI, Equinix's retail colocation the further. Iron Mountain sits at the edge: records storage is the bulk of the company and the data-center business is one reported segment with its own revenue and EBITDA, which makes it the one landlord with a segment to read. Miners converting sites into leased shells (Applied Digital, Core Scientific) do the same thing from the other side; they sit in `miner_to_hpc`.

Equinix (EQIX). Segments are Americas, EMEA and Asia-Pacific (Q2 2026: $1,251M, $845M, $529M revenue); no AI or hyperscale segment. 2025 revenue $9.217 billion; 2025 purchases of PP&E $4,311 million plus $994 million of real estate. 2026 capex guidance as of 29 July 2026: total $5.000 to 6.000 billion, recurring $290 to 310 million, non-recurring $4.710 to 5.690 billion, the non-recurring line excluding xScale and real estate. The only stated AI share is qualitative: about 60% of the largest Q4 2025 deals were "driven by AI workloads". Not disclosed as of 29 October 2026: AI or hyperscale share of capex or revenue, xScale megawatts leased in the quarter (the 134 MW figure in search summaries is not in the release).

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Capex by type** (`facts`, MD&A): "expansion" or "non-recurring" or "development" capex versus "recurring" or "maintenance". Expansion capex is new capacity, which since 2023 is overwhelmingly AI-driven, but the company rarely says how much is AI.

## How to attribute

Capex, in order of hardness:

- `segment`: Iron Mountain's data-center segment capex when the filing gives it, with `basis` saying that this is data-center capacity, not AI specifically.
- `stated_amount` / `stated_share`: when the company states an AI or hyperscale part of development capex. None of the three had done so as of 29 October 2026.
- `whole_business` is not allowed: a data-center REIT's capex is data-center capex, but data-center is not AI. Use `qualitative` with confidence ≤ 0.5 when the company links the development pipeline to AI demand (Equinix's "60% of largest deals driven by AI workloads" is the kind of statement that earns it).
- `none` otherwise.

Opex: `none`.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_share` / `stated_amount`: only when the company states AI's or hyperscale's part of revenue or of new leasing; confidence ≤ 0.6, and new leasing is not revenue in the year (say so). Digital Realty's hyperscale lease dollars ($410 million annualized in July 2026) are leasing, not revenue.
- `segment`: Iron Mountain's Global Data Center segment revenue (read it from the 10-K segment note), confidence ≤ 0.5, with `basis` "data-center rent, not AI". For Equinix and Digital Realty the data-center business is the whole company, so a segment says nothing about AI; do not use it.
- `qualitative`: leasing demand attributed to AI in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3. The usual answer for Equinix and Digital Realty.
- `none`: when nothing links rent to AI.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a campus or building with a location and megawatts or an amount, a joint venture with capital raised for named development, or a hyperscale lease with a size: a named campus under construction, an xScale or hyperscale JV, a land purchase with planned megawatts, a pre-lease to a hyperscaler. Words that name one: "campus", "megawatts", "under construction", "pre-leased", "joint venture", "promote", "land", "phase", "development pipeline" when sites are named. Not a project: an interconnection or cloud-exchange product, a new market entry with no site, a rate increase, a hire.

Named projects as of 29 October 2026: Equinix's xScale JV program ($15 billion of JV capital, Hampton, Georgia contributed in January 2026; new projects in Chicago, Istanbul and Johor in Q2 2026); Digital Realty's three Northern Virginia buildings (288 MW, about $7.8 billion gross) and Kansas City land (about $475 million); Iron Mountain's 325 MW energization program and the 10 MW Amsterdam lease.

- Expansion capex equals data-center capex, which is broader than AI. Never equate the two without a statement.
- Joint ventures (xScale, DLR's hyperscale JVs) carry capex off balance sheet; "net of partner contributions" in guidance means the gross build is larger. Note it in `basis`.
- Promote income (DLR's $188 million in Q2 2026) is a development fee, not rent and not AI revenue.
- Leasing signed in the year is backlog, not revenue; a record leasing quarter is a project signal, not a revenue row. Backlog at 100% share and at the company's share are different numbers; record which.
- Iron Mountain's segment revenue is data-center rent; its ceiling is capped for the same reason as its capex.
- Guidance raised twice in a year (both Equinix and Digital Realty in 2026) is the plans-versus-reality signal; record each revision with its date.

# Thesis: power producer (power@v3)

## Thesis

Independent power producers sell electrons, and their AI story is data-center load: nuclear restarts and uprates, gas plants co-located with data centers, long-term PPAs with hyperscalers. Project-level investment is the measure that matters: the AI link lives in a named plant with a named counterparty. Capex allocation matters only for growth capex the company itself ties to such a project; the rest is generation, transmission and fuel. Plans versus reality matters for growth capex guidance. Revenue exposure does not matter: power sold under a hyperscaler PPA is still power, and no segment is the AI one. The signal to watch is contracted data-center megawatts with a counterparty and a date, and whether the capex that serves them has started.

The backdrop is real load growth. LBNL's report for the DOE (December 2024) put US data-center use at 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of US electricity) and projected 325 to 580 TWh by 2028 (6.7% to 12%). That is why the PPAs below exist; it is not evidence that any one producer's capex is AI.

## Companies

Vistra (VST), Constellation (CEG), NRG (NRG) and Talen (TLN). None of the four reports an AI or data-center segment. Vistra reports Retail, Texas, East, West and Asset Closure; Talen reports PJM and All Other; no segment is by customer. What each has stated:

Constellation (CEG). Two named nuclear PPAs. Crane Clean Energy Center (the former Three Mile Island Unit 1, 835 MW) under a 20-year PPA with Microsoft signed September 2024; restart target 2027, about $1.6 billion of restart investment, backed by a $1 billion DOE Loan Programs Office loan closed November 2025. Clinton Clean Energy Center under a 20-year PPA with Meta for 1,121 MW starting June 2027, with a 30 MW uprate (release of 3 June 2025; the release does not use the words data center, but Meta's quote ties it to "our AI ambitions"). The Q2 2026 release (6 August 2026) adds 920 MW of new 15 to 20 year nuclear PPAs starting 2029 to 2032 with unnamed investment-grade customers, plus 176 MW to Walmart; it gives no data-center capex figure and no capex guidance. Not disclosed as of 29 October 2026: any AI or data-center share of capex or revenue.

Talen (TLN). One named project. The FY2025 10-K (Item 1) states a fixed-price PPA to supply AWS up to 1,920 MW from Susquehanna through 2042, ramping to full volume no later than 2032. Utility Dive (11 June 2025) reports the ramp as 840 to 1,200 MW in 2029 and 1,680 to 1,920 MW in 2032, an estimated $18 billion of revenue over the contract life per Talen's investor deck, and the shift of the 300 MW co-located arrangement to a front-of-the-meter structure. The 2024 sale of the adjacent data campus to AWS is the origin of the arrangement. Not disclosed as of 29 October 2026 in the filing text read: a data-center capex amount.

Vistra (VST). The Q4 2025 release (26 February 2026) states a 20-year PPA with AWS for up to 1,200 MW at Comanche Peak (power delivery from 2027 per Utility Dive, 10 August 2026, which also reports Amazon's $5 billion data center next to the plant), 20-year PPAs with Meta for more than 2,600 MW of energy, capacity and uprates across its PJM nuclear fleet, and a 200 MW solar PPA with AWS at Oak Hill. 2025 capex was $2,752 million including nuclear fuel and LTSA prepayments, with $1,348 million maintenance and $1,126 million growth and development; 2026 guidance is $1,536 million total. The release does not split growth capex by customer or project. Not disclosed: any AI or data-center share of capex or revenue.

NRG (NRG). No nuclear. Its data-center story is a 295 MW long-term power agreement for new data centers on two company-owned Texas sites (first power second half 2026, full by 2030, per Power Engineering, 6 August 2025, counterparty not named), a stated 445 MW of contracted data-center capacity and 4 GW of letters of intent (Utility Dive, 17 November 2025), the GE Vernova and Kiewit development agreement for about 5.4 GW of gas plants (1.2 GW by 2029, 1.2 GW by 2030, 3 GW 2030 to 2032) with 2.4 GW of turbine slots reserved, and the roughly $12 billion LS Power acquisition of about 13 GW of gas. Management said in November 2025 that a data-center agreement tied to the gas build would come in 2026; none was found by 29 October 2026. Not disclosed: a capex amount for the gas plants or an AI share of anything.

Regulated utilities that serve data centers are not in the set; neither are the fuel-cell and turbine makers, who sit in `datacenter_build`.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **What the company says** (`ai_spend`): named projects with a data-center counterparty ("Crane Clean Energy Center restart for Microsoft", "Susquehanna campus for Amazon", "Comanche Peak PPA with AWS"), growth capex guidance tied to data-center demand.
2. **Capex by category** (`facts`, MD&A): "growth" versus "maintenance" or "nuclear fuel". Vistra reports this split; growth capex tied to a named data-center project is attributable.
3. **Segment capex** (`facts.segment_capex`): by generation fleet or market, never by customer.

## How to attribute

Capex, in order of hardness:

- `stated_amount`: a capex amount the company ties to a data-center project or PPA (`scope: ai` or `scope: datacenter`). Crane's $1.6 billion restart is the one such amount in the set, and it is a restart cost spread over 2024 to 2027, not a year's capex; take the year's share only when the filing gives it.
- `qualitative` with confidence ≤ 0.4 when growth capex is linked to data-center demand in words only (Vistra's growth and development capex, NRG's gas build).
- `none` otherwise, which is the common answer.

Opex: `none`.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_amount` / `stated_share`: only when the company states revenue under data-center PPAs for the year; confidence ≤ 0.5, with `basis` "contracted power to a data-center customer, not AI revenue". A contract's total value (Talen's $18 billion over the life of the AWS PPA) is not revenue in the year. None of the four had stated such a figure as of 29 October 2026.
- `segment`: not available. Generation and market segments (Vistra's Texas and East, Talen's PJM) are not data-center lines; never sum them.
- `qualitative`: load growth or pricing attributed to data-center demand in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3.
- `none`: the common and honest answer.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a plant with a counterparty, a size and a date: a nuclear restart or uprate under a hyperscaler PPA, a gas plant built or co-located for a named data-center customer, a PPA with megawatts and a term, a data-center campus on company land with a development partner. Words that name one: "power purchase agreement", "restart", "uprate", "co-located", "behind the meter", "front of the meter", "megawatts", "gigawatts", "20-year", "campus", "slot reservation", "letter of intent" with a counterparty. Not a project: a fuel contract, a rate case, a hedging statement, a share buyback, a hire.

Named projects as of 29 October 2026: Crane (CEG, Microsoft, 835 MW, 2027), Clinton (CEG, Meta, 1,121 MW plus 30 MW uprate, June 2027), Susquehanna (TLN, AWS, up to 1,920 MW through 2042), Comanche Peak (VST, AWS, up to 1,200 MW, from 2027), Vistra PJM nuclear (Meta, more than 2,600 MW), NRG Texas sites (295 MW, counterparty not named) and the NRG gas build (5.4 GW with GE Vernova and Kiewit, no data-center customer named yet).

## Traps

- A restart or uprate serving the grid is not AI capex because a hyperscaler signed a PPA; only capex the company itself ties to the counterparty counts.
- Nuclear fuel purchases are not growth capex. Vistra's capex totals include nuclear fuel and LTSA prepayments; strip them before reading growth.
- A PPA's contract value over twenty years is a project amount, not revenue in the year.
- Megawatts in a release can be a contract ceiling ("up to 1,200 MW"), a ramp step, or an aggregate across plants ("more than 2,600 MW"); record which.
- A letter of intent (NRG's 4 GW) with no megawatts contracted or site is a plan, not a project; record it as `qualitative` in the project's status, not as a row with an amount.
- A PPA release that never says "data center" (Constellation's Clinton and Q2 2026 PPAs) is still a data-center link only when the counterparty is a hyperscaler; for unnamed investment-grade customers it is `none`.

# Thesis: AI software and data platform (ai_software@v3)

## Thesis

Software and data platforms rent their compute from the hyperscalers, so AI shows up as cloud purchase commitments and hosting cost of revenue, not as capex. Capex allocation matters only when a company states it buys its own GPUs; the committed cloud spend is the real number and it sits in `basis`, not in the year's spend. Revenue exposure matters, but only through what the company states about AI products, and most state ARR, ACV or bookings rather than revenue. Project-level investment is the cloud commitments themselves; plans versus reality rarely applies. The signal to watch is the step-up in purchase commitments year on year, which is the committed AI compute, read against stated AI product revenue or ARR. Two numbers set the scale in 2026: Salesforce's $16.7 billion of commitments to infrastructure providers at 31 January 2026 against $594 million of capex, and Snowflake's $6 billion five-year AWS commitment (May 2026) against product revenue of about $6 billion a year.

## Where the AI money shows up

1. **Purchase commitments** (`facts.purchase_commitments`): multi-year cloud commitments with AWS, Azure, Google Cloud; the step-up since 2023 is AI compute. Committed, not spent. Salesforce $16.7 billion total (10-K, January 2026); Snowflake $6 billion over five years with AWS (May 2026).
2. **Cost of revenue and R&D** (`ai_spend`, MD&A): "increased hosting costs for AI features", "AI model training costs in R&D". Opex, rarely quantified. Snowflake's product gross margin guide of 74.0% is the visible trace.
3. **Capex** (`values.capex`): small, usually offices and equipment (Salesforce $594 million for a year, Palantir $14.6 million for a quarter); AI only when the company states it buys its own GPUs, which none of the six did in the releases read.
4. **Stated AI product figures** (`ai_spend`): AI ARR (Salesforce $800 million Agentforce), AI ACV (ServiceNow $1 billion), AI-first ARR growth (Adobe, percent only), account counts for an AI product (Snowflake CoCo and CoWork).

## How to attribute

Capex: `stated_amount` / `stated_share` only when the company states an AI part; otherwise `none`, the 2026 answer for all six.

Opex: `stated_amount` when a release or MD&A gives an AI hosting or compute figure; `qualitative` with confidence ≤ 0.4 when cost of revenue growth or gross margin is attributed to AI in words; `none` otherwise.

Record the cloud purchase commitments in `basis` as the committed AI compute, never in `ai_amount` (they are not spend in the year). Salesforce's $16.7 billion covers all infrastructure providers, not AI alone; say so.

Revenue, in order of hardness:

- `stated_amount`: the company states AI product revenue for the year; confidence ≤ 0.8. None of the six did as of 29 October 2026. An ARR or ACV figure (Salesforce's $800 million Agentforce ARR, ServiceNow's $1 billion AI ACV) is not fiscal-year revenue: confidence ≤ 0.5 and name the measure in `basis`. A growth rate with no base (Adobe's AI-first ARR up more than 150%) is not an amount: `qualitative`. "AI-influenced" ARR, where stated, counts deals that include AI, not AI revenue: ≤ 0.3.
- `stated_share`: the company states AI's share of revenue, ARR or bookings; same ceilings as above by measure. ServiceNow's target of AI at 30% of ACV by 2030 is a plan, not a share.
- `segment`: not available. Palantir's US commercial and US government are not AI lines; Adobe's customer groups and Salesforce's clouds are not AI lines. Never sum one as the AI revenue.
- `qualitative`: growth attributed to AI products in words only, confidence ≤ 0.3. The 2026 answer for Snowflake ("meaningful step-up in AI revenue"), Palantir and Datadog.
- `none`: nothing stated.
- `whole_business`: never.

## Projects

A project is a committed, sized spend on AI compute: a multi-year cloud commitment with a named hyperscaler and amount, a stated purchase of the company's own GPUs or a data center, a sized investment program the company names ("$N billion over five years" for AI infrastructure). Words that name one: "commitment", "non-cancelable", "agreement with" a cloud provider, "GPUs", "data center", "invest $" with a term. Not a project: a product launch (an agent, a copilot, a model), an AI feature release, a partnership with no amount, an acquisition, a hire.

Named as of 29 October 2026: Snowflake's $6 billion AWS commitment over five years (27 May 2026). Salesforce's $16.7 billion of infrastructure commitments is a total across providers with no named project; record it in `basis`.

## Traps

- A cloud commitment is committed spend across several years, not capex and not this year's opex.
- "AI revenue" (AI product ARR) is the sales side, not spend; it belongs in the revenue field, with the ARR ceiling.
- ARR, ACV, bookings, RDV, TCV and "AI-influenced" are each a different thing from revenue; name which one was stated and cap the confidence. Palantir's $6.238 billion of US commercial RDV is a backlog of all deals, not AI revenue.
- A customer-count, account-count or "deals including AI" statement is qualitative, not a share.
- Call-only figures (Datadog's AI-native cohort, Snowflake's AI share of acceleration) are not in the releases; cite the call or stay at the release's ceiling.
- ARR that includes an acquisition (Salesforce's $2.9 billion includes $1.1 billion of Informatica) is not organic AI growth.
